newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazilian TV shows new scenes of police violence.
newsitem.headline: Brazilian TV shows new scenes of police violence.

text.p: Brazilian television showed new images of police violence on Monday just one week after a videotape of officers beating drivers outraged a nation already accustomed to police brutality.
An amateur videotape taken at the end of March and screened on Monday by Globo television showed military policemen beating a group of men lined up against a wall in a poor Rio de Janeiro suburb.
None of the men showed any act of provocation or violence as the police whipped them with belts and beat them with a heavy piece of wood.
One man, who had fainted, failed to get up after a police officer poured some water over him. The policeman threw the plastic bottle at him, whipped him with a belt and kicked him.
The man finally got up, stumbled to the wall and was then subjected to a further whipping.

Another man endured a particularly harsh beating. Forced to hold out his hands to be hit by one policeman, another pummeled his back and head. Globo said the man needed surgery to recover his hearing.
During the tape, the only noise to break the thud of flesh being beaten was the occasional sound of music coming from nearby bars.
The men were eventually released as the police had no cause to detain them.
"They didn't even ask what we were doing ... They took our money, they took 10 reais ($9.50) from my pocket and 20 from my friend," said one 18-year old interviewed by Globo.

The video was taken by a man whose brother had earlier been subjected to police violence, Globo said. "I felt indignation. It's horrible to see them act like that. It's not what you expect from the police," the man told Globo, his face hidden from the camera.
One week ago Globo aired another videotape showing military police in Sao Paulo beating drivers at a roadblock and firing at a car. One passenger later died.

The officers have since been arrested and the public outcry that followed the tape prompted President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to sign a decree establishing a human rights watchdog and sanction a bill making torture a crime for the first time.

In an interview with weekly Veja magazine published on Sunday, Cardoso said police violence in Brazil was a cultural problem. "We are in a country which has always tended to accept police violence. There is no law that can change this," he said.
Rio de Janeiro state governor Marcello Alencar pledged to take swift action after seeing the latest tape with the state public security chief and the head of the military police.
"The governor has recorded the tape which will now be analysed to determine the identity of the policemen involved, who will then be arrested," spokesman Antonio Cunha told Reuters.
